articles.summary:

Gross GST collections from domestic sales rose 16 per cent to over Rs 1.59 lakh crore, and revenues from imports climbed 42 per cent to Rs 72,246 crore.
The Rs 2.31 lakh crore collection includes Central GST mop-up of 42,935 crore, State GST of Rs 51,340 crore and Integrated GST of over Rs 1.37 lakh crore, data showed.
Goods and Services Tax (GST) refunds increased 6.5 per cent year-on-year to Rs 27,934 crore in October.
After adjusting for refunds, net GST collections rose 26 per cent to over Rs 2.03 lakh crore in October.
During April-October, gross GST collection grew 13.2 per cent to over Rs 14.77 lakh crore. Net collections rose 13 per cent to over Rs 12.69 lakh crore.

articles.title: AI bargains with AI: The next great bazaar
articles.summary: In the market, humans meet humans to buy, sell and make deals. The next great bazaar may be where our Al agents haggle for milliseconds Walk through any Indian bazaar and bargaining is de rigueur. The shopkeeper names a price with wounded dignity, the buyer laughs derisively, threatens to walk away, comes back, talks about another shop and, eventually, both parties settle somewhere between offence and satisfaction. The transaction seems purely economic, but it is also social, rich in stories and psychological and emotional, and very human.Now imagine if neither of them is human.Also read: E-commerce firms turn to AI to solve for Bharat during festive salesYour AI agent has already discovered the product, compared alternatives, checked reviews and decided what you are willing to pay. The seller's AI knows inventory, margins, demand and how badly it needs the sale. The two agents bargain for milliseconds, settle on a price and complete the transaction. You receive a message: "Bought it. Saved you 12%."This is no longer science fiction. Personal agents such as Instinct, Meta's Muse and Open AI's Dots are moving AI from answering questions to doing things on our behalf, as you move from asking the AI to tasking the AI.Muse can browse, book and buy with permission. Instinct, which lives inside your WhatsApp, can arrange travel, buy groceries and manage subscriptions.Open AI's Dots are designed as always-on agents with their own cloud computers and access to connected applications. These are early steps towards what an agent really means: software to which we give agency.Also read: AI-aided gifting, self-love light up Zoomer DiwaliEra of negotiationThe next step is obvious. Why merely search and buy when the agent can negotiate? That possibility has moved from speculation to serious research. The Financial Times recently reported that Anthropic is consulting lawyers on how AI agents should negotiate for users, including prices, contracts and disputes.Experiments found that more aggressive agents sometimes got better outcomes, while cooperative ones occasionally gave up individual advantage to reach an agreement. Visa is already talking about "business-to-AI" commerce; more than half the business leaders it surveyed said they were ready for AI-to-AI negotiation.This could change commerce more profoundly than another shopping chatbot.First, the internet itself will have to change. Amazon, Flipkart, or a B2B procurement platform, is designed today to persuade humans. There are glossy pictures, seductive descriptions, stories, influencer videos, recommendations and carefully designed buttons. Machines care much less about romance. An agent wants structured facts: price, dimensions, warranty, delivery time, return policy, reliability, compatibility and perhaps the seller's willingness to negotiate.Two facesWebsites may therefore acquire two faces: one for humans, rich in stories and emotion, and another for machines, factual, structured and instantly comparable. Search engine optimisation gave us SEO. Agentic commerce may give us something like AEO: agent-engine optimisation. The next customer arriving at your website may never see the website.Bargaining itself becomes democratised. There are people who hate negotiating. A skilled agent could give an ordinary consumer some of the power previously available mainly to corporations and wealthy people - a tireless professional negotiator that knows when to push, when to walk away and what alternatives exist.But that creates a new inequality. What happens when my agent is smarter than yours? The wealthy have always hired better lawyers, brokers and advisers. If the richest people also subscribe to the most capable negotiating models, AI might not remove bargaining inequality but actually industrialise it.This is where John Nash and his famous work on game theory enter the bazaar. Game theory studies how rational actors behave when each person's outcome depends partly on what others do. A Nash equilibrium occurs when neither side gains by changing strategy alone.Human negotiators reach such equilibrium imperfectly, clouded by emotion, incomplete information and ego. AI agents could run thousands of strategies almost instantly.Collusion ConundrumBut there is a darker version. What if the buyer's agent and seller's agent learn that subtle cooperation is more profitable for both agents? Perhaps that is the choice ahead. Agents will increasingly represent us because, for many transactions, they will simply be better at it. They will know our budgets, preferences and histories, and eventually negotiate with other agents that know equally much about the other side.Algorithmic pricing has already raised concerns about tacit collusion. A world of autonomous negotiators makes the question sharper: whose interests are they really optimising?And then there is something less economic but perhaps equally important. Humans like shopping. We wander through bazaars, browse bookstores, discover things we did not know we wanted, argue over carpets and feel triumphant when a shopkeeper finally gives us "the special price only for you". Shopping is not merely procurement. It is entertainment, discovery, status, ritual and human contact.If my agent buys my airline ticket, insurance policy and printer cartridge, I will probably be delighted. If it chooses every restaurant, negotiates every holiday and buys every gift, I may have outsourced not just inconvenience but part of life itself.Perhaps that is the choice ahead. Agents will increasingly repre-sent us because, for many transactions, they will simply be better at it. They will know our budgets, preferences and histories, and eventually negotiate with other agents that know equally much about the other side.The bazaar will not disappear. It may split in two. In one, humans will still wander, haggle, flirt with choices and occasionally overpay for the pleasure of the experience. In the other, invisible agents will negotiate billions of transactions at machine speed.For thousands of years, the market was where humans met humans to bargain. The next great bazaar may be where our machines meet instead.

articles.summary: New Delhi: Above-normal maximum temperatures are likely over most parts of India in November, except for some regions along the foothills of the Himalayas where normal to below-normal maximum temperatures are expected, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Saturday in its monthly forecast.It also stated that during the month, above-normal minimum temperatures are expected over most parts of the country, except in many parts of central and eastern India where normal to below-normal minimum temperatures are likely.The IMD noted that in November, below-normal rainfall is likely over most parts of the country except for some areas in central, northwest, and Northeast India, where normal to above-normal rainfall is likely.India as a whole is likely to witness 77 per cent of Long Period Average (LPA) rainfall during the month.LPA refers to the rainfall recorded over a particular region for a given interval, such as a month or season, averaged over a long period, typically 30 to 50 years. The LPA of rainfall over the country during the month of November, based on data from 1971 to 2020, is about 29.7 mm.South Peninsular India is also likely to experience 77 per cent of LPA during November. The LPA of rainfall over the region during November, based on data from 1971 to 2020, is around 118.7 mm, according to the IMD.The department highlighted that currently, very strong El Nino conditions are prevailing over the Equatorial Pacific Ocean.The latest Monsoon Mission Coupled Forecast System (MMCFS) and other global climate model forecasts indicate that very strong El Nino conditions are likely during November-December.El Nino is one of the three phases of the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a climate phenomenon characterised by changes in sea temperatures along the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, accompanied by fluctuations in the atmosphere overhead.While El Nino is known to have a warming effect over the planet, its opposite phase, La Nina, usually results in a cooling effect. ENSO also has a neutral phase.Very strong El Nino conditions could be one of the key reasons why during this year's October, India witnessed the highest monthly average maximum temperature (32.43 degrees Celsius) since 1901. The normal monthly average maximum temperature for October is 31.37 degrees Celsius, according to the IMD.Moreover, the monthly average minimum temperature during this October was the fifth highest (20.83 degrees Celsius) since 1901. articles.title: Silver loses more than half its value from record high: What went wrong and will it recover?
articles.summary: After years of lagging behind gold and trading in a broad consolidation range, silver staged an exceptional rally this year, surging to a record high of nearly $120 an ounce in the London spot market in February. Domestic prices in India also scaled unprecedented levels, supported by robust industrial demand, tight supplies, strong investment inflows, and speculative buying. The rally briefly made silver one of the best-performing commodities and attracted significant investor participation.However, the uptrend proved unsustainable. Following its historic peak, silver entered a prolonged correction as investor optimism faded amid profit-booking, slower industrial demand growth, and changing macroeconomic conditions. Prices gradually retreated throughout the year and slipped to $50 an ounce this week, marking a decline of more than 58% from the February high. The sharp reversal has reignited concerns over the durability of silver's bull run. Although long-term demand from renewable energy and electronics remains supportive, the market is increasingly reassessing growth expectations and pricing in a more cautious outlook amid global economic uncertainty.Why did silver prices reach a record high?Silver's rally to record highs was fueled by a combination of strong industrial demand, tightening supplies, and robust investment inflows. Demand from solar panels, electric vehicles, semiconductors, and advanced electronics surged, reinforcing silver's role as a critical industrial metal. At the same time, persistent supply deficits emerged as mine production struggled to keep pace with growing consumption.On the investment side, silver benefited from rising concerns over inflation, currency weakness, mounting government debt, and geopolitical uncertainties, prompting investors to increase exposure to precious metals. The metal also rode on gold's bullish momentum, attracting speculative buying due to its smaller market size and higher volatility. Expectations of monetary easing by major central banks further boosted investor appetite. With strong industrial consumption coinciding with tight physical supplies and increased fund participation, silver prices rallied sharply, reaching record highs in both international and Indian markets earlier this year.Why have silver prices fallen so sharply this year?The sharp correction in silver prices reflects a significant reassessment of the bullish expectations that had driven the metal to record highs earlier this year. Following the rally, extensive profit-booking by hedge funds, institutional investors, and speculative traders accelerated the decline. Industrial demand growth also fell short of the lofty projections priced into the market, as weaker economic activity in major consuming regions, particularly China and Europe, weighed on manufacturing demand.A stronger US dollar and periods of elevated real interest rates further reduced the appeal of non-yielding assets such as silver. Investment demand weakened as exchange-traded funds (ETFs) witnessed outflows, with investors reallocating funds to cash and fixed-income assets. Meanwhile, some industrial consumers postponed purchases in anticipation of lower prices. The combination of long liquidation, softer industrial demand, and changing macroeconomic conditions resulted in silver prices losing more than half of their value from the peak reached earlier this year.How is the supply-demand scenario?Despite the sharp correction in prices, the global silver market continues to face a relatively tight supply-demand balance. Demand remains supported by the growing use of silver in solar panels, electric vehicles, electronics, batteries, and medical applications, making it one of the most important industrial precious metals. However, supply growth has been limited, as a large portion of global silver output is produced as a by-product of lead, zinc, copper, and gold mining, restricting producers' ability to quickly increase production in response to price movements.That said, weakening economic growth and lower prices are expected to moderate industrial demand in the near term. At the same time, increased recycling activity could add secondary supply to the market. While supply deficits may persist, the imbalance appears less severe than earlier anticipated, reducing some of the bullish momentum that had previously supported silver prices.Investment demand and why geopolitical tensions have not supported silverSilver occupies a unique position as both a precious and industrial metal, but during periods of geopolitical uncertainty investors generally favour gold over silver. Gold enjoys stronger safe-haven credentials, deeper liquidity, lower volatility, and continued purchases by central banks, making it the preferred defensive asset during times of crisis. As a result, much of the safe-haven capital generated by geopolitical tensions this year has flowed into gold rather than silver.At the same time, silver's heavy dependence on industrial demand has limited its appeal. More than half of global silver consumption comes from industrial applications, making the metal vulnerable to concerns about slowing economic growth and weaker manufacturing activity. Consequently, while geopolitical tensions have supported precious metals in general, concerns over slowing industrial demand have largely offset any safe-haven buying in silver, keeping prices under sustained pressure.Outlook: Why a break below $50 could be significantThe $50-per-ounce level is emerging as a key psychological and technical support for silver. A sustained break below this threshold could trigger fresh selling from speculative funds and momentum traders, increasing downside pressure. The sharp correction from this year's record highs suggests the market is moving away from the highly bullish environment that previously supported prices. While long-term demand from solar energy, electric vehicles, semiconductors, and green technologies remains constructive, these factors may not be sufficient to support prices in the near term. If global growth remains weak and investment demand fails to recover, silver could remain vulnerable to further declines. Therefore, long-term investors may consider waiting for price stabilization before building fresh positions.(The author  is Head of Commodity Research, Geojit Investments Limited)(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by the experts are their own. Oregon midair helicopter collision kills three
articles.summary: An experienced pilot was on a test run in a helicopter and a 22-year-old flight instructor with a student pilot from the United Kingdom were in another when the two aircraft collided midair in Oregon and crashed into a farm field, killing all three.Details about the three victims were still emerging Friday, as the National Transportation Safety Board said a team was on its way to examine the wreckage from the previous day's crash. Law enforcement photos showed a red helicopter lying crumpled in a farm field, while a green helicopter came to rest upside down.The crash happened around 2 p.m. Thursday on a cloudy day, a few miles east of the airport in McMinnville. The town, about an hour's drive southwest of Portland, lies in the broad, flat Willamette Valley near the foothills of the Coast Range, in the heart of Oregon's wine country.Leo Rodriguez was working on a nearby barn roof at his family's winery when the helicopters collided."There was an explosion mid-air," he told KPTV. "I bent over to do something and then, boom, and I look up and the planes were already going down."Rodriguez said the tail end of the larger helicopter was struck, then it turned and began going toward the ground. He said the other helicopter fell straight down."It just happened so fast," he said.Few details were immediately available about the collision. The smaller Robinson R22 helicopter was on an instructional flight, according to the NTSB. The Airbus AS350B3 helicopter was on a maintenance flight, which are typically done after maintenance or repair.The victims included 38-year-old Tyler Sturdevant, a pilot from Oregon, 22-year-old Maddie Aasbo, a flight instructor from Texas, and 31-year-old Christopher Joughin, a student pilot from the United Kingdom, Yamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott said during a news conference.Aasbo graduated from the wildlife management program of Southwest Texas College, in Uvalde, and was a member of its rodeo team from 2021 to 2023, according to a post on the group's Facebook.The post described her as a brave, bold and independent woman who also worked for large hunting ranches in Texas and spent time in New Mexico and Alaska. In Oregon, the group said, she "had found ultimate freedom in the air as a helicopter pilot and instructor.""Her sudden passing has left us equally stunned and heartbroken," it said. "It is beyond difficult to find the words worthy of a young woman of her caliber and impact-fulness."The owners of the two helicopters - Jerry Trimble Helicopters and Precision - both said they are cooperating with authorities on the investigation while trying to help the grieving families of the victims.Precision, a helicopter charter and maintenance company that also helps fly drone missions for the military, said in a post on Instagram that Sturdevant was their "beloved" senior pilot."Tyler has touched countless lives, not only through his love of flying, but through the many pilots he mentored, encouraged, and helped along the way," Precision posted. "His legacy lives on in every pilot he helped bring up and every life he made a difference in."His LinkedIn page says he worked as a pilot examiner for the Federal Aviation Administration for the past four years while continuing to work at Precision for more than 20 years.In 2021, Sturdevant's wife, Monica Sturdevant, nominated him as a community hero on an Oregon Facebook group. She described him as a great husband and father who missed celebrating Father's Day with them that year because he was helping fight forest fires.She also said he signed up to be an Angel Flight pilot in his free time to help transport people to important medical appointments."He's not doing it for recognition, or because he expects anything in return, but simply because of his compassion for people, and I couldn't be more proud of him," Sturdevant said.The U.K.'s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said in a statement that it was in touch with local authorities and providing support to Joughin's family.The Jerry Trimble school offers everything from demo flights for first-time flyers to advanced training.

articles.title: Startup bug bites fewer IIT, IIM alumni
articles.summary: New Delhi: Fewer graduates from Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) and Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs) are taking the entrepreneurial path in 2026 compared to last year, although India's appetite for startups remains strong.Only 79 IIT alumni and 20 IIM alumni launched new tech startups between January and August this year, compared to 307 IIT graduates and 71 IIM graduates who founded startups in the entire 2025, according to Tracxn data collated for ET. The platform tracks only the year of incorporation for tech startups, so it does not have comparable January-August 2025 data.Also Read: Not Just AI - How soft skills are becoming key to getting hiredFurther, according to Tracxn data, 6,353 tech startups were founded until August this year, compared with 3,969 in the whole of 2025."The increase in the number of startups being founded is a positive sign, but the real question is who is making that transition. The fact that we are not seeing a meaningful increase in founders from the IITs and IIMs suggests there is still a large, untapped pool of talent," said Vikram Gupta, founder and managing partner, IvyCap Ventures.Also Read: Centre to tap IITs, NITs for nuclear tech courses to power India's 100 GW dream135376542AI & Layoffs as Decisive Factors"If India wants to build the next generation of enduring companies, entrepreneurship must become a more viable career choice for a much wider talent pool," Gupta said.According to Saakshi Gera, managing director at Kedaara Capital, startups are increasing largely because artificial intelligence (AI) and no-code tools have dramatically reduced the cost of launching a venture, while layoffs have made entrepreneurship a more viable fallback option."But volume isn't quality. Investors continue to prioritise sustainable unit economics, and India's most credentialed talent is increasingly choosing safer, AI-adjacent jobs instead," Gera said.More IIT graduates take the entrepreneurial route than IIM alumni. articles.title: US stocks slide: Amazon, Intel, Nvidia fall
articles.summary: US stock market today: US stocks fell for the second day in a row on Friday, October 30, as investors worried about the health of the AI trade. At 10:58 AM ET, the Dow Jones was at 52,113.50, down 229.06 points or 0.44%. The S&P 500 was at 7,621.06, down 99.33 points or 1.29%. The Nasdaq was at 25,623.29, down 561.44 points or 2.14%.Why is the US stock market down today?Two earnings reports, from Amazon and Intel, came after Thursday’s closing bell and are pulling the market down this morning.Thursday was already weak. All three major indexes closed lower, and the Nasdaq lost 1.6% after Alphabet’s results disappointed. Amazon and Alphabet both posted rare earnings misses. Alphabet had its worst day in over 20 years.Amazon missed estimates on both revenue and profit. Its free cash flow also fell because of heavy spending on AI. Intel dropped sharply after giving a weak outlook for the fourth quarter.Chip stocks fell across the board. AMD lost 9%, Marvell 6% and Broadcom 5%. Micron and Nvidia each gave up more than 3%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX), which holds Intel and AMD as its two biggest positions, was down 7%.Crypto stocks also took a hit. Bitcoin fell to around $76,600 from a high near $82,000 on Thursday. Strategy (MSTR) was down 10%, Coinbase (COIN) 12% and Robinhood (HOOD) 8%.In other markets, WTI crude was above $104 a barrel, up about 2%. Gold fell to around $3,920, close to its lowest level since last November. The 10-year Treasury yield stayed at 4.94%.Intel stock price today: why the chipmaker is down nearly 30%Intel (INTC) is the worst performer on the S&P 500 today. At 10:58 AM ET it traded at $66.52, down $25.55 or 27.75%. Earlier in the session it fell about 30%, to below $65. That is a price the stock has not seen since spring.The fall comes after a big run. Intel was up roughly 250% this year through Thursday’s close, and had recently crossed levels last seen in 2000.The trigger was the company’s outlook. Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and GAAP profit of 10 cents a share. Both are below the average estimate tracked by Visible Alpha. This overshadowed third-quarter numbers that were better than expected. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the company faces “headwinds across the PC industry” and is finding it hard to meet “extremely high AI driven demand.”Intel’s foundry business, which makes chips for other companies, is also under watch. Its revenue rose nearly 60% year on year in Q3, but it posted an operating loss of nearly $1.9 billion.Valuation is another worry. Before the fall, Intel traded at more than 50 times estimated 2027 earnings, well above its peer group average. Morgan Stanley, which rates the stock neutral, cut its price target to $75 from $84. The Visible Alpha average target is around $90.High trending stocks today: Amazon, Nvidia, Reddit and moreAmazon (AMZN) traded at $239.31, down 1.84%. Third-quarter revenue rose nearly 12% from a year ago to about $202 billion. Net income fell, partly because last year’s quarter had gains from its stake in Anthropic. Amazon still expects AWS revenue growth run rates above 40% in both 2027 and 2028. The stock is up just 3% this year, while the S&P 500 is up 11%.Nvidia (NVDA) was at $207.25, down 3%. Alphabet (GOOGL) was at $280.64, down 1.12%, and CoreWeave (CRWV) was at $55.48, down 8.65%. SpaceX (SPCX) was at $138.52, down 3.73%, and Nokia (NOK) was at $8.66, down 6.98%.Three internet stocks also fell after their Q3 results. Reddit (RDDT) dropped 24%, Roblox (RBLX) 16% and Pinterest (PINS) 6%.Acumen Pharmaceuticals (ABOS) fell 87.47% to $0.29.A few stocks rose. TNL Mediagene (TNMG) gained 24.26% to $3.79 and Rivian (RIVN) added 5.41% to $12.07.
